fallback_summary_en: Languages do not all package one versus more than one in the same way. Some require singular/plural marking, some also distinguish a dual or other number values, and some often leave noun number unmarked and rely on context, numerals, classifiers, articles, particles, or agreement.

transparency_slide.description: The lesson is one declarative multilingual shell layered with language-specific number-system data. The app owns the universal lesson runner; this family never assumes that every language has the same number categories or marks them in the same place.
transparency_slide.rendering_model: Render the learner's best language first using its native comparison record, then the selected learning language. Additional known languages may be added in profile order. Each record owns its number-system forms and own_grammar_blurb; never infer a singular/plural binary from English.

support_selection.full: Render the native comparison block, structured GrammarRuleBlock sections, curated examples when available, and defensible rule-driven practice.
support_selection.comparison_only: Render the native comparison block only. Do not synthesize target-language rules or practice.
support_selection.unavailable: Keep a product-known language discoverable but omit unsupported lesson content.

number_system_model.topic: grammatical number in noun phrases and agreement
number_system_model.teaching_rule: Describe the target language's real inventory and obligatoriness. Never force every language into singular versus plural, and never confuse grammatical number with numeric counting or CLDR plural categories.

eligibility.source_language_policy: Every language in programs.learnFromLanguages may be used as a source/comparison language when its native comparison record is present.
eligibility.target_language_policy: Only current Tier 1 and Tier 2 grammar languages may be selected as learning targets for this lesson.

block_plan.notes: Introduce grammatical number without assuming a universal binary. Use one/more-than-one as an intuitive starting point, then explicitly allow dual, optional marking, and other systems.
Show each language's representative number categories or marking strategy and its own_grammar_blurb in that language. The learner's native language comes first, followed by the learning language.
Explain three separate questions: which number meanings the language distinguishes, whether nouns must mark them, and where agreement or number marking appears.
Render structured target-language rules from GRAMSET.mul.grammatical_number. Tier membership alone is not a rule source.
Prefer reviewed corpus examples when available. The English-to-Spanish reference lesson may use the structured Spanish worked examples embedded in the rendering until corpus examples are available.
Transition into target-language number choices only when a unique, defensible answer exists.
Practice number formation and agreement from structured rules. Do not generate a fake singular/plural choice for languages where the noun can legitimately stay unmarked.
Offer a reading quest to notice number marking and agreement in real text when the target language has a meaningful visible distinction.
Reinforce that number is a language-specific grammatical system, not a word-for-word translation rule.

learning_path_policy.notes: Tier 1 may eventually place this in a complete grammar path. Tier 2 may place it selectively. Tier 3 can still explain the learner's source-language system but is not a grammar-learning target.
